content: Childhood cancer survivors face an increased risk of developing chronic health conditions, such as osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease, compared to their peers. Engaging in health-promoting behaviors, such as maintaining a healthy diet, has the potential to mitigate these risks. However, the prevalence of such behaviors among childhood cancer survivors is comparable to that of the general population. Nutritional interventions specifically tailored to this group may help prevent or reduce the incidence of these chronic diseases. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various nutritional interventions aimed at improving the dietary intake of childhood cancer survivors, compared to a control group that did not receive such interventions. Secondary objectives included assessing metabolic and cardiovascular risk factors, weight and body fat distribution, behavioral changes, knowledge about disease risk and nutrition, participants' perceptions of the interventions, health status and quality of life, potential harms associated with the interventions, and their cost-effectiveness. To identify relevant studies, electronic databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE/PubMed, and Embase were searched up to April 2013, with an additional search conducted in August 2015. Ongoing trial registers, reference lists of relevant articles, and conference proceedings were also reviewed. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing nutritional interventions with control groups were included. Participants were childhood cancer survivors diagnosed before the age of 18 and who had completed curative treatment prior to the intervention. Data from eligible studies were independently extracted and assessed by two reviewers using standardized forms. The quality of the studies was evaluated using the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and the GRADE criteria. Three RCTs, involving a total of 616 participants, met the inclusion criteria. One study focused on survivors of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), while the other two included survivors of various pediatric cancers. Participants were under 21 years of age at the start of the studies, and follow-up periods ranged from one month to 36 months. The studies evaluated different interventions, making it impossible to pool the results. Bias could not be ruled out in any of the studies. One study assessed a single, half-day, group-based education session on bone health. At one month, there was no clear evidence of a difference in calcium intake between the intervention and control groups (mean difference [MD] 111.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] -258.97 to 482.17; P = 0.56; low-quality evidence). However, regression analysis, adjusted for baseline calcium intake and changes in knowledge and self-efficacy, showed a significantly greater calcium intake in the intervention group at one month (beta coefficient 4.92, 95% CI 0.33 to 9.52; P = 0.04). Participants in the intervention group also reported significantly higher milk consumption (MD 0.43, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.79; P = 0.02; low-quality evidence), more days of calcium supplementation (MD 11.42, 95% CI 7.11 to 15.73; P < 0.00001; low-quality evidence), and greater use of calcium supplements (risk ratio [RR] 3.35, 95% CI 1.86 to 6.04; P < 0.0001; low-quality evidence). There was no clear evidence of a difference in bone density Z-scores at 36 months between those who received calcium and vitamin D supplementation combined with nutrition education and those who received nutrition education alone (MD -0.05, 95% CI -0.26 to 0.16; P = 0.64; moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, no significant differences in bone mineral density were observed at 12 months (median difference -0.17; P = 0.99) or 24 months (median difference -0.04; P = 0.54). Another study evaluated a multi-component health behavior change intervention focused on general healthy eating principles, with two follow-up telephone sessions. This intervention resulted in a statistically significant reduction in self-reported junk food intake (MD -0.17 on a four-point Likert scale, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.01; P = 0.04; low-quality evidence). However, there was no clear evidence of a difference in the self-reported use of nutrition as a health-protective behavior (MD -0.05, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.14; P = 0.60; low-quality evidence). The authors concluded that due to the limited number of studies and their heterogeneity, no definitive conclusions could be drawn about the effectiveness of nutritional interventions for childhood cancer survivors. While there is low-quality evidence suggesting that health behavior change interventions may improve health behaviors, there is no evidence to confirm that these changes lead to improved dietary intake. Additionally, there is no evidence that these interventions reduce the risk of cardiovascular or metabolic disorders in this population. However, the absence of evidence does not equate to evidence of no effect. The review underscores the need for well-designed trials to further investigate this area.
